cells.tense: You are clearing what needs to end, and it has your full attention now.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Pick one yes-or-no in what you're clearing and sit with it ten minutes before acting. Note where you finally draw the line. That's the whole practice.
cells.core:
Something is ending, and you can feel the shape of what comes after without having built it yet. The clearing isn't a crisis; it's bench work. You take what stays and what goes apart carefully, and you are careful rather than fast. That care is the practice itself.

The distinction you make this week will hold. Refine one of them by close attention: sit with a single yes-or-no, look at it long enough to see the grain, and mark the line where you draw it. What goes, goes clean; what stays, stays because you looked. You don't need to hurry the ending to prove it happened.
cells.sheetLine: You're clearing what needs to end, and the clearing is the craft.
cells.verb: Deepening a dedicated craft through persistent building.
cells.place: Where necessary endings and clearing are underway.

cells.tense: You will have cleared it all by some future date, and you are bracing for that day now.
cells.act: let the gladness go out to the room
cells.ask: Say what's good about this clearing where someone can hear it. Not the plan — the gladness. Speak it before the work is done.
cells.core:
You are clearing instead of clearing out? Reconsider. Actually: You are clearing a space, and the ending has a deadline only you can see. The finished version stands built ahead of you, so today's work feels late. The ending gets bigger as the days get closer, and you brace for a date that hasn't arrived.

Let the gladness go out to the room before the last box is packed. Say what's actually good about this ending where someone can hear it — the space it makes, the weight it lifts — and don't wait for the work to be done to say it. Mark the good part early, out loud, with whoever is near. The good part is real now, not after.
cells.sheetLine: You're clearing toward a future, and bracing for it.
cells.verb: Deepening a dedicated craft through persistent building.

cells.tense: You were standing at a door that has already closed, and you are still standing there.
cells.act: state the order of things once, without argument
cells.ask: Put the order of one thing on the table out loud — what stays, what has gone — with no explanation after it. One sentence, then stop.
cells.core:
The ending already happened where you are. What is left is the clearing, and the clearing keeps getting postponed because naming it would make it real. You know the shape of it. You have not put the shape on the table.

State the order of things once, without argument. Say what has ended and what is still here in one plain sentence, out loud, and don't defend it or soften it. A frame that is spoken stops being fog. You don't have to feel finished to say a thing is finished. Say it once and trust the words to carry it.
cells.sheetLine: You were at a door that closed, and you are still at it.
cells.verb: Deepening a dedicated craft through persistent building.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room you are already writing, and you haven't noticed.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Choose the pace of this clearing you could keep for a month, and hold it this week. Nothing faster. Just the rhythm you can carry.
cells.core:
You are already clearing something, and it is happening from a feeling you haven't named. The work and the pull travel the same direction without your having decided it. That quiet is why the momentum can run without you watching it. You have been treating it as busy, or as just what needed doing.

Do the next piece at the pace you can keep for a month, not the pace you can keep for a day. Hold that rhythm this week. Don't surge to catch up; don't stop to explain. A steady pace is what turns quiet momentum into a road. What feels like managing the ending is the direction you've been giving it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already clearing, and the pace is yours to set.
cells.verb: Deepening a dedicated craft through persistent building.

attempts.check: The reading most exposed to challenge is calling the person steady under weight in the Balanced cell; the record supports the capacity but not the outside view that others feel the floor hold. The ask still works if the read is wrong — honing one distinction is useful to anyone clearing space, and it never asks them to feel steady. The sentence that serves me more than them is the 'ages of clear thinking' image, which sounds like craft and could be said about anyone in a threshold; the Too Much cell drops it and stays with the kitchen-table description of clearing. The Too Little cell's claim that the door is 'still the whole exit' is hedged out of any explanation of why, so the person can reject the history and keep the practice.
